laws.title: Hands-Free Driving Law
laws.subtitle: CT Code §14-296aa — No handheld devices while driving
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut prohibits holding or using handheld electronic devices while driving. Handheld device use while driving is banned.
laws.penalty: $150 first, $300 second, $500 third.
laws.exceptions: Emergency 911 calls are exempt from hands-free requirements.

quiz.q: Is handheld phone use banned while driving in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: all handheld device use while driving is banned statewide.

laws.title: Non-Resident Hunting & Fishing License
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §26-28 — Non-residents must purchase licenses
laws.fullDescription: Non-residents must obtain a valid Connecticut hunting or fishing license before taking game or fish. Annual non-resident fishing licenses cost approximately $19; hunting licenses cost approximately $135. Some species require additional tags.
laws.penalty: Class B misdemeanor or felony; fines up to $1000 plus equipment forfeiture.
laws.exceptions: Residents are exempt from non-resident fees.

quiz.q: What is the penalty for hunting without a license in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Hunting without a license in Connecticut is a Class B misdemeanor with fines up to $1000.

laws.title: Impaired Driving (DUI/DWI)
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §14-227a — 0.08% BAC limit
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut prohibits operating a vehicle with a BAC of 0.08% or higher. Commercial drivers: 0.04%. Drivers under 21: 0.02 BAC. Implied consent laws apply.
laws.penalty: First offense: $500–$1,000 fine, 45-day license suspension, up to 6 months jail. Subsequent offenses carry mandatory minimums and longer suspensions.
laws.exceptions: None — even prescription medication impairment can result in DUI charges.

quiz.q: What BAC triggers a DUI in Connecticut for regular drivers?
quiz.explanation: The legal BAC limit in Connecticut is 0.08% for regular drivers, consistent with all US states.

laws.title: Open Container Law
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §30-130 — No open alcohol in vehicles
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut prohibits open alcoholic beverage containers in the passenger area of motor vehicles on public roads. Open container law applies to driver and passengers.
laws.penalty: $150 fine; applies to driver and passengers.
laws.exceptions: Passengers in for-hire vehicles (taxis, limos) may be exempt.

quiz.q: Can passengers drink alcohol in a private car in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut's open container law applies to all vehicle occupants.

laws.title: Recreational Cannabis — Legal
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §21a-420a — Recreational cannabis legal — adults 21+
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Connecticut legalized recreational cannabis in 2021 (Public Act 21-1). Adults 21+ may possess up to 1.5 oz in public. Licensed dispensaries sell recreational products.
laws.penalty: Public consumption: $50 fine. Possession over limits: misdemeanor.
laws.exceptions: Medical patients may possess larger amounts.

quiz.q: Is recreational cannabis legal in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut legalized recreational cannabis in 2021 for adults 21+.

laws.title: Medical Cannabis — Legal
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §21a-408 — Medical cannabis program
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut has had a medical cannabis program since 2012. Registered patients may possess a 30-day supply.
laws.penalty: Non-patients face criminal charges.
laws.exceptions: Registered patients are exempt from possession penalties.

quiz.q: Does Connecticut have a medical cannabis program?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut has a medical cannabis program.

laws.title: Firearm Carry Law — Shall-issue
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §29-28 — Shall-issue state
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut is a shall-issue state. Connecticut requires a permit to carry a handgun. Permits are issued to all qualified applicants. Background check and safety course required.
laws.penalty: Carrying while prohibited: felony.
laws.exceptions: Firearms prohibited in schools, courts, and government buildings.

quiz.q: What type of carry law does Connecticut have?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut has shall-issue — permits required; issued to all qualified applicants meeting all requirements

laws.title: Background Check Requirements
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §18 USC 922 — Federal NICS checks at licensed dealers
laws.fullDescription: All firearm purchases from licensed dealers in Connecticut require a federal NICS background check. Connecticut requires background checks for all handgun transfers, including private sales.
laws.penalty: Straw purchases or sales to prohibited persons: federal felony up to 10 years.
laws.exceptions: Transfers between immediate family members may be exempt.

quiz.q: Does Connecticut require background checks for private gun sales?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut requires background checks for all gun sales.

laws.title: Stand Your Ground / Castle Doctrine
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Criminal Code — Castle Doctrine only
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut has a Castle Doctrine — force is justified inside the home, but there is a duty to retreat outside the home before using deadly force.
laws.penalty: N/A — this law provides a defense against criminal charges.
laws.exceptions: Force not justified if defender is committing a crime or the intruder is a co-resident.

quiz.q: Does Connecticut have a Stand Your Ground law?
options: No — duty to retreat outside home
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Duty to retreat exists outside the home — Castle Doctrine only in Connecticut.

laws.title: Minimum Wage Law
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Labor Code — $15.69/hour minimum wage
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut's minimum wage is $15.69/hour (2024). Connecticut tied its minimum wage to the Employment Cost Index, making it one of the first states with an automatic cost-of-living adjustment for minimum wage.
laws.penalty: Employers violating minimum wage: back wages, double damages, and attorney fees.
laws.exceptions: Tipped workers may have a lower base wage.

quiz.q: What is the minimum wage in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut's minimum wage is $15.69/hour.

laws.title: At-Will Employment
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Labor Code — Employment at will doctrine
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut follows at-will employment. Employers may terminate for any legal reason; employees may quit anytime. at-will employment with standard exceptions.
laws.penalty: N/A — at-will is the default standard.
laws.exceptions: Termination for illegal reasons (discrimination, retaliation) is prohibited.

quiz.q: Can an Connecticut employer fire an employee without giving a reason?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut is an at-will employment state — employers may generally terminate without cause.

laws.title: Right-to-Work Law — No
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Labor Code — Connecticut is NOT a right-to-work state
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut is not a right-to-work state. Connecticut is not a right-to-work state. Union security agreements are permitted.
laws.penalty: N/A — this governs labor relations framework.
laws.exceptions: Federal employees and some categories are governed by federal law.

quiz.q: Is Connecticut a right-to-work state?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut is NOT a right-to-work state.

laws.title: Non-Compete Agreement Enforceability
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Business Code — Non-compete enforceability rules
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Non-compete agreements enforced if reasonable in scope and duration.
laws.penalty: Overly broad agreements may be voided or reformed by courts.
laws.exceptions: Agreements protecting legitimate trade secrets are most favored.

quiz.q: Are non-compete agreements automatically enforceable in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Courts assess reasonableness of non-competes.

laws.title: Paid Sick Leave — Required
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §31-57r — 5 paid sick days required
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Connecticut requires employers with 50+ employees to provide 5 paid sick days per year. Employees earn 1 hour per 40 hours worked.
laws.penalty: Violation: civil fines and back pay.
laws.exceptions: Independent contractors are generally not covered.

quiz.q: Does Connecticut require employers to provide paid sick leave?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Connecticut requires up to 5 paid sick days for eligible employees.

laws.title: Unemployment Insurance
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Labor Code — Unemployment benefits
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut unemployment insurance provides benefits to eligible workers. Maximum weekly benefit: $773 for up to 26 weeks. Workers must have earned at least $600 in the base period.
laws.penalty: Filing fraudulent claims: repayment plus penalties and possible criminal charges.
laws.exceptions: Self-employed and independent contractors are generally ineligible for regular UI.

quiz.q: What is the maximum weekly unemployment benefit in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut's maximum weekly unemployment benefit is $773.

laws.title: Workers' Compensation
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Labor Code — Mandatory workers' comp coverage
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut requires employers with 1 or more employees to carry workers' compensation insurance. Covers medical costs and lost wages for work-related injuries.
laws.penalty: Employers without coverage: fines up to $5000/day, personal liability for claims.
laws.exceptions: Sole proprietors and some domestic workers may be exempt.

quiz.q: How many employees trigger workers' comp requirements in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut requires workers' comp for employers with 1 or more employees.

laws.title: Independent Contractor Classification
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Labor Code — Worker classification rules
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut uses Common law control test to classify workers. Worker classification uses the common law control test.
laws.penalty: Misclassification: back taxes, penalties, and retroactive benefits liability.
laws.exceptions: Licensed professionals may have different classification standards.

quiz.q: What test does Connecticut use for worker classification?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut uses the Common law control test for worker classification.

laws.title: Child Labor Laws
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Labor Code — Restrictions on youth employment
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut restricts employment of minors. Children under 14: very limited jobs only. Ages 14–15: restricted hours. Most minors under 18 need work permits. Federal child labor protections apply with state additions.
laws.penalty: Employers violating child labor laws: fines up to $10000 per violation.
laws.exceptions: Family farms and limited entertainment work have exemptions.

quiz.q: At what age do minors generally need work permits in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Most Connecticut minors under 18 need work permits for regular employment.

laws.title: Equal Pay Act
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §46a-60 — Equal pay for equal work
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut prohibits pay discrimination based on sex for substantially equal work. Connecticut Fair Employment Practices Act prohibits sex-based wage discrimination.
laws.penalty: Back pay, compensatory damages, and attorney fees for violations.
laws.exceptions: Pay differences justified by seniority, merit, or non-sex factors are permitted.

quiz.q: What agency enforces equal pay laws in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut's civil rights agency and the federal EEOC both enforce equal pay laws.

laws.title: Anti-Discrimination in Employment
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §46a-60 — Protected classes in Connecticut
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut prohibits employment discrimination based on race, religion, color, national origin, sex, age (40+), disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, and marital status. Connecticut has broad anti-discrimination protections including explicit LGBTQ+ coverage.
laws.penalty: Compensatory damages, back pay, reinstatement, and attorney fees.
laws.exceptions: Religious organizations may have limited exemptions for certain positions.

quiz.q: How many employees must an Connecticut employer have before anti-discrimination laws apply?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut anti-discrimination laws apply to employers with 3 or more employees.

laws.title: Landlord Entry Notice Requirement
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §47a-16 — reasonable notice (typically 24)-hour notice required
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut landlords must give tenants reasonable notice (typically 24) hours' written notice before entering for non-emergency purposes. Entry must be at reasonable times.
laws.penalty: Unlawful entry may entitle tenant to damages or lease termination.
laws.exceptions: Emergencies (fire, flood, imminent harm) allow immediate entry without notice.

quiz.q: How many hours notice must Connecticut landlords give before entering?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut landlords must give reasonable notice (typically 24) hours' notice before non-emergency entry.

laws.title: Security Deposit Rules
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §47a-21 — Two months' rent maximum deposit
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Maximum security deposit is Two months' rent. Deposits must be returned within 30 days of move-out with an itemized statement of deductions.
laws.penalty: Landlord who wrongfully withholds deposit may owe double damages plus attorney fees.
laws.exceptions: Deposits for pets may be separate in some cases.

quiz.q: How many days does a Connecticut landlord have to return a security deposit?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut landlords have 30 days to return security deposits after move-out.

laws.title: Rent Control Status — Not Statewide
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Housing Code — No statewide rent control
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Connecticut has no statewide rent control, though some localities have explored it.
laws.penalty: N/A — this is a policy/regulatory matter.
laws.exceptions: Federally subsidized housing has separate rent rules.

quiz.q: Does Connecticut have statewide rent control?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: No statewide rent control in Connecticut.

laws.title: Eviction Process & Tenant Protections
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Landlord-Tenant Act — Notice and court process required
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut landlords must provide: 3 days notice for nonpayment; 15 days for violations; 3 days for no-cause termination. Court filing required after notice expires.
laws.penalty: Self-help eviction (changing locks, removing belongings) is illegal.
laws.exceptions: Emergency situations may allow expedited proceedings.

quiz.q: How many days notice for non-payment of rent before eviction in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut requires 3 days notice for nonpayment of rent before filing for eviction.

laws.title: Short-Term Rental (STR) Regulations
laws.subtitle: Local codes — Regulated locally
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: STR regulations vary by municipality.
laws.penalty: Operating without required licenses: fines and possible closure.
laws.exceptions: Owner-occupied properties renting a single room may have reduced requirements.

quiz.q: Are short-term rentals (Airbnb) regulated in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut regulates STRs primarily at the local level with varying requirements by city.

laws.title: Property Tax
laws.subtitle: Local codes — Average 1.73% effective rate
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Average effective property tax rate is approximately 1.73%. Connecticut has some of the highest property taxes in the US, partly offsetting its lack of estate tax.
laws.penalty: Delinquent taxes accrue interest and may result in tax lien or foreclosure.
laws.exceptions: Senior citizens and disabled veterans often receive exemptions. Senior and veteran exemptions available.

quiz.q: What is the approximate average effective property tax rate in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut's average effective property tax rate is approximately 1.73%.

laws.title: Homestead Exemption
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §12-81 — $1,000 assessment reduction (modest) homestead exemption
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Connecticut's homestead exemption is modest compared to other states, providing a small reduction in assessed value for primary residences.
laws.penalty: N/A — this is a protection for homeowners.
laws.exceptions: Does not protect against tax liens, mortgage foreclosures, or mechanic's liens.

quiz.q: What is Connecticut's homestead exemption?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut's homestead exemption is $1,000 assessment reduction (modest).

laws.title: State Income Tax — Yes — graduated 3–6.99%
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §12-700 — Yes — graduated 3–6.99%
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Connecticut has a graduated income tax ranging from 3% (low incomes) to 6.99% (high incomes).
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: civil penalties, back taxes, and possible criminal charges.
laws.exceptions: Federal income taxes apply to all residents regardless of state income tax.

quiz.q: Does Connecticut have a state income tax?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Connecticut has a graduated income tax with rates from 3% to 6.99%.

laws.title: Sales Tax Rate
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Revenue Code — 6.35% statewide sales tax
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut has a 6.35% statewide sales tax. Local taxes add to the state rate. Combined state and local rates average 6.35%.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: civil penalties and criminal charges for substantial violations.
laws.exceptions: Exempt items typically include: Groceries, prescription drugs, and most clothing under $50..

quiz.q: What is the statewide sales tax rate in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut's statewide sales tax is 6.35%.

laws.title: Estate / Inheritance Tax — Yes
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §12-391 — Yes — estate tax on estates over $13.6M
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Connecticut imposes an estate tax on estates over $13.61 million (2024), with rates up to 12%. Connecticut is one of the few states still with an estate tax.
laws.penalty: N/A — federal estate tax applies to all US residents with large estates.
laws.exceptions: Federal estate tax applies to estates over $13 million (2024).

quiz.q: Does Connecticut have a state estate or inheritance tax?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Connecticut imposes an estate tax on large estates — top rate of 12%.

laws.title: Smoke-Free Workplace Law
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Health Code — Clean Air Act / Smoke-Free law
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut prohibits smoking in enclosed workplaces, restaurants, and bars.
laws.penalty: Violation: $100–$500 per incident for individuals.
laws.exceptions: Some private clubs and outdoor areas may be exempt.

quiz.q: Is smoking banned in workplaces and restaurants in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Comprehensive smoke-free law covers most indoor workplaces.

laws.title: Motorcycle Helmet Law
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Vehicle Code — Universal helmet law
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: All motorcycle operators and passengers must wear helmets in Connecticut.
laws.penalty: Helmet violation: $100 fine.
laws.exceptions: N/A

quiz.q: Who must wear a motorcycle helmet in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Universal helmet law.

laws.title: Seatbelt Law
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Vehicle Code — Mandatory seatbelts
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut requires all front-seat occupants to wear seatbelts. Children under 8 or under 60 lbs must be in child safety seats.
laws.penalty: $25 fine for violations; higher for child restraint violations.
laws.exceptions: Some commercial vehicles and emergency situations may have limited exemptions.

quiz.q: Is the seatbelt law a primary offense in Connecticut?
options: Yes, police can stop for seatbelt alone
quiz.explanation: Connecticut's seatbelt law is a primary enforcement offense.

laws.title: Speed Limits
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Vehicle Code — Statutory speed limits
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Residential: 25 mph; highways: 65 mph; interstates: 65 mph; school zones: 20 mph. Posted limits vary.
laws.penalty: Speeding fines start at $50 and increase with severity; reckless driving is a criminal charge.
laws.exceptions: Emergency vehicles are exempt when responding.

quiz.q: What is the interstate speed limit in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut's standard interstate speed limit is 65 mph.

laws.title: Texting While Driving
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Vehicle Code — Texting while driving banned
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Texting while driving is prohibited.
laws.penalty: First offense: $150; repeat: $300.
laws.exceptions: Emergency 911 calls are permitted while driving.

quiz.q: Is texting while driving banned in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Connecticut bans all handheld device use while driving.

laws.title: DUI Checkpoint Legality
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Vehicle Code — Sobriety checkpoints permitted
laws.fullDescription: DUI sobriety checkpoints are legal in Connecticut. DUI checkpoints legal with proper procedures.
laws.penalty: N/A — this defines when checkpoints are legal.
laws.exceptions: Checkpoints must follow established procedures to be constitutional.

quiz.q: Are DUI sobriety checkpoints legal in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: DUI checkpoints are legal with proper procedures.

laws.title: Move Over Law
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Vehicle Code — Slow or move over for emergency vehicles
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut's Move Over Law requires drivers to change lanes or slow down when passing stopped emergency vehicles and tow trucks and highway maintenance vehicles with flashing lights on the roadway or shoulder.
laws.penalty: Violation: $100 fine; if injury or death results, criminal charges may apply.
laws.exceptions: Required only when safe to do so without creating greater hazard.

quiz.q: Does Connecticut's Move Over Law cover tow trucks?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut's Move Over Law covers tow trucks.

laws.title: Cell Phone Use While Driving
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §14-296aa — Handheld device restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Beyond texting, Connecticut bans all handheld device use while driving including phone calls.
laws.penalty: Fines range from $150 to $500.
laws.exceptions: Hands-free calls and navigation use are generally permitted.

quiz.q: Can drivers make calls on a handheld phone while driving in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Handheld phone restrictions apply while driving.

laws.title: Age of Majority
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Civil Code — Age 18 is legal adulthood
laws.fullDescription: In Connecticut, the age of majority is 18. At 18, residents gain the right to vote, enter contracts, and make their own legal decisions. Age-specific restrictions still apply.
laws.penalty: N/A — this defines civil rights.
laws.exceptions: Some rights have higher age thresholds: alcohol (21), cannabis where legal (21).

quiz.q: What is the age of majority in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut's age of majority is 18, consistent with most US states.

laws.title: Voting Rights & Restoration
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §9-12 — Voter eligibility and felon restoration
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Felons may register to vote and vote after release from prison. Connecticut restored voting rights for people on parole in 2021.
laws.penalty: Voting while ineligible (while incarcerated): criminal charge.
laws.exceptions: Mentally incapacitated persons adjudicated incompetent may lose voting rights.

quiz.q: When are voting rights restored to a felon in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Connecticut restored voting rights upon release from prison in 2021.

laws.title: Jury Duty Requirements
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Court Rules — Jury service
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut citizens who are US citizens, 18+, registered voters (or driver's license holders) may be called for jury duty. Jurors receive $50/day. Employers must allow employees to serve.
laws.penalty: Willfully ignoring a jury summons: contempt of court, fines up to $500.
laws.exceptions: Exemptions include active military, police, extreme hardship, and some medical conditions.

quiz.q: What is the daily pay for jurors in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut jurors receive $50 per day for service.

laws.title: Mandatory Reporting of Child Abuse
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Child Welfare Act — Mandatory reporters
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Designated professionals are mandatory reporters. Reports must be made to child protective services or law enforcement. Good-faith reporters are protected from liability.
laws.penalty: Failure to report known child abuse: misdemeanor.
laws.exceptions: Attorney-client privilege may apply in limited circumstances.

quiz.q: Who must report suspected child abuse in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Designated professionals must report suspected child abuse.

laws.title: Age of Consent
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §53a-71 — Age of consent is 16
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut's age of consent is 16. Age of consent is 16 with a 2-year age-gap provision for 15-year-olds. Sex offenders must register with the state registry.
laws.penalty: Sexual abuse of a minor: Felony; sex offender registration..
laws.exceptions: Romeo and Juliet provision: Persons aged 15 may consent to sex with partners within 2 years of their age..

quiz.q: What is the age of consent in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut's age of consent is 16.

laws.title: Emancipation of Minors
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Family Code — Court-ordered emancipation
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut allows minors aged 16+ to petition for emancipation, granting adult legal status. The court considers whether it's in the minor's best interests and whether the minor can support themselves.
laws.penalty: N/A — emancipation is a civil court process.
laws.exceptions: Emancipation does not override minimum age laws for alcohol, cannabis, or voting.

quiz.q: At what minimum age can a minor petition for emancipation in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut allows minors aged 16+ to petition for emancipation.

laws.title: Curfew Laws for Minors
laws.subtitle: Local codes — Local ordinances only
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: No statewide curfew; municipalities set their own rules.
laws.penalty: Curfew violation: minor taken into custody and released to parents; parents may face fines.
laws.exceptions: Minors with employment, parental supervision, or school activities are typically exempt.

quiz.q: Does Connecticut have a statewide youth curfew?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Curfews set locally.

laws.title: Corporal Punishment in Schools
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Education Code — Corporal punishment prohibited
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Corporal punishment is prohibited in all Connecticut public schools.
laws.penalty: Educators using prohibited corporal punishment face administrative discipline and potential criminal charges.
laws.exceptions: Physical restraint to prevent imminent harm is permitted.

quiz.q: Is corporal punishment allowed in Connecticut public schools?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Corporal punishment prohibited in public schools.

laws.title: Homeschooling Regulations
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Education Code — Homeschooling requirements
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Families must notify the superintendent and provide instruction covering required subjects. Annual assessment or portfolio review.
laws.penalty: Failure to provide required education: mandatory enrollment in public school.
laws.exceptions: Some states have additional oversight or assessment requirements.

quiz.q: Does Connecticut have strict homeschooling regulations?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut has moderate-regulation homeschooling with moderate requirements with notification and required subjects.

laws.title: School Vaccination Requirements
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Health Code — Required vaccinations for school entry
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut requires students to be vaccinated against standard childhood diseases for school entry. Standard vaccinations required for school entry.
laws.penalty: Unvaccinated students without exemptions may be excluded from school.
laws.exceptions: Exemptions available: medical and religious exemptions (philosophical removed 2021).

quiz.q: Can Connecticut parents claim a philosophical exemption from school vaccinations?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut vaccination exemptions: medical and religious exemptions (philosophical removed 2021).

laws.title: Abortion Laws
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §19a-116 — Legal — protected by state law
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Abortion is legal in Connecticut. State law (PA 90-113) protects abortion rights up to viability and beyond for health of the mother. Connecticut also provides safe haven for out-of-state patients.
laws.penalty: N/A — abortion is fully protected.
laws.exceptions: Medical emergencies to save the life of the mother are typically exempt.

quiz.q: What is the gestational limit on abortion in Connecticut?
options: Up to viability (~24 weeks) and beyond for health
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Abortion is legal in Connecticut through viability and beyond for health reasons.

laws.title: Death Penalty — Abolished
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §53a-54b — Death penalty status
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut does not have the death penalty. Connecticut abolished the death penalty in 2012 (prospectively). The state carried out its last execution in 2005.
laws.penalty: Maximum punishment is life without parole.
laws.exceptions: Federal death penalty may apply to federal crimes regardless of state law.

quiz.q: Does Connecticut have the death penalty?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Connecticut abolished the death penalty in 2012.

laws.title: Medical Aid in Dying (MAID)
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §53a-56 — Assisted suicide illegal
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Medical aid in dying is not yet legal in Connecticut. Legislation has been debated.
laws.penalty: Assisting a suicide is a felony.
laws.exceptions: Withdrawal of life support and palliative sedation are legal with patient consent everywhere.

quiz.q: Is medical aid in dying (assisted suicide) legal in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Medical aid in dying is not legal in Connecticut.

laws.title: Drug Penalties (Non-Cannabis)
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §21a-279 — Controlled Substances Act
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut controlled substance penalties: Drug possession penalties: small amounts of cannabis are civil infractions; hard drugs (heroin, meth, cocaine) are felonies with diversion programs for first-time offenders.
laws.penalty: Possession of hard drugs: misdemeanor to felony. Distribution/manufacture: felony up to 30 years.
laws.exceptions: Prescribed medications used as directed are exempt.

quiz.q: Is simple drug possession a felony in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Drug penalties vary by substance and amount.

laws.title: Asset Forfeiture Laws
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Criminal Code — Civil asset forfeiture
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Connecticut allows civil asset forfeiture. Reforms have increased some protections.
laws.penalty: N/A — forfeiture is an action against property.
laws.exceptions: Innocent owner defense available: property returned if owner proves no criminal connection.

quiz.q: Does Connecticut require a criminal conviction before forfeiture?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Civil forfeiture allowed without conviction.

laws.title: Expungement & Record Sealing
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Criminal Code — Expungement availability
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Connecticut expanded expungement in 2021 — many misdemeanors and some felonies can be erased after waiting periods.
laws.penalty: N/A — this is a post-conviction relief process.
laws.exceptions: Serious felonies, sex offenses, and violent crimes generally cannot be expunged.

quiz.q: Can first-time non-violent offenders expunge their records in Connecticut?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Limited expungement available.

laws.title: Solitary Confinement Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Corrections Code — Restricted housing policies
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: DOC policies limit solitary confinement use.
laws.penalty: N/A — this governs prison administration.
laws.exceptions: Extremely dangerous inmates may face longer restricted housing.

quiz.q: Has Connecticut restricted the use of solitary confinement?
quiz.explanation: Connecticut: Limited reforms on solitary confinement.

laws.title: Private Prison Use
laws.subtitle: Conn. Gen. Stat. §Corrections Code — Private correctional facilities
laws.fullDescription: Connecticut: Some private facilities used.

quiz.explanation: Connecticut officers may use deadly force only when reasonably necessary to prevent death or serious injury.

laws.fullDescription: Connecticut has a Red Flag (ERPO) law. Connecticut was the first state to enact an ERPO law (1999). Risk warrants allow temporary firearm removal from dangerous individuals.

laws.title: Hate Crime Laws
